findings.claim: The first drug information centre opened at the University of Kentucky Medical Center in 1962, not 1960.
findings.evidence: "First DIC was developed in University of Kentucky in 1960."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Say 1962, University of Kentucky Medical Center.

findings.claim: The claim that 80% of US hospitals have a DIC is unsourced; most hospitals provide drug information through pharmacists, and the number of formal centres has fallen.
findings.evidence: "In United states 80% of the Hospitals having DIC."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Drop the percentage; say that formal centres are fewer today and most drug information is given by pharmacists at the point of care.

findings.claim: The Egyptian drug information centre date is given without a source.
findings.evidence: "Egyptian drug information center (EDIC) establishment was organized in 2012"
findings.source: Egyptian Drug Authority website (edaegypt.gov.eg)
findings.fix_hint: Keep only if confirmed from the EDA; otherwise describe the EDA drug information and pharmacovigilance services without a date.

findings.claim: The online-source examples are misclassified or out of date: MEDLINE is a secondary (indexing) database, TOXNET was retired in 2019, and the FDA site and DailyMed hold official labelling, not summaries.
findings.evidence: "Medscape® / TOXNET from NIH / Medline from NIH / FDA website / Daily Med (side effects)" under "Electronic and Online tertiary information resources"
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022; NLM Technical Bulletin 2019 (TOXNET retirement)
findings.fix_hint: Tertiary online: Micromedex, Lexicomp, UpToDate, Medscape. Secondary: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase. Official labelling: DailyMed, Drugs@FDA, EDA. Drop TOXNET.

findings.claim: Randomisation gives a known chance, equal only in 1:1 allocation; the next slides teach unequal allocation. 'Predicated' should be 'predicted'.
findings.evidence: "Randomization gives each participant a known and equal chance ... cannot be predicated in advance."
findings.source: CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869
findings.fix_hint: "Each participant has a known chance (equal in 1:1 allocation) of each group, and the next assignment cannot be predicted."

findings.claim: The listed 'disadvantages of randomisation' are limitations of controlled trials (efficacy vs effectiveness, strict criteria), not of randomisation itself.
findings.evidence: "Trials which test for efficacy may not be widely applicable."
findings.source: CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869
findings.fix_hint: Rename as 'Limitations of randomised controlled trials' and explain efficacy (ideal conditions) vs effectiveness (real practice) in one table.

findings.claim: A trial never proves the null hypothesis; it tests H0 and either rejects it or fails to reject it.
findings.evidence: "So, in a clinical trial we proof the concept relying on the H0 hypothesis."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: "H0 says there is no difference. The trial tests H0: if p < alpha we reject H0; otherwise we fail to reject it. Failing to reject is not proof of no difference."

findings.claim: Alpha is the significance level (false-positive risk), not 'precision'; 1 - alpha is the confidence level. Alpha 5% and beta 20% are conventional choices set by the investigator, not fixed facts.
findings.evidence: "Error type 1 (Alpha) : affects precision of the clinical study. The possibility of error type 1 ( False positive) to occur is 5% So, The precision is 95% ."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Use a 2x2 table (truth vs decision): type I = false positive, alpha usually set at 0.05; type II = false negative, beta usually 0.1-0.2; power = 1 - beta (80-90%).

findings.claim: The IRB definition is taken from a science-fair context ('fair, high school'); it does not describe the ethics committee of a clinical trial.
findings.evidence: "A committee of specific composition at an affiliated fair, high school, or institution that reviews research plans"
findings.source: ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, 2025
findings.fix_hint: "An independent committee that reviews and approves a trial protocol and consent form, and monitors the trial, to protect the rights, safety and well-being of participants."

findings.claim: Informed consent is defined as permission to process personal data (a data-protection definition), not the voluntary agreement of a trial participant after full disclosure.
findings.evidence: "Informed consent means asking the data subject for permission before a process ... how it will be processed."
findings.source: ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, 2025
findings.fix_hint: "A participant's voluntary, documented agreement to take part, given after being told the purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and alternatives, and that they can withdraw at any time."

findings.claim: A secondary outcome is also pre-specified in the protocol; it is not any additional outcome that 'occurs' during the study.
findings.evidence: "Secondary Outcome: is the additional outcome that occurs during the study."
findings.source: CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869
findings.fix_hint: "Secondary outcomes are pre-specified outcomes of lesser importance; outcomes found only after the data are seen are exploratory."

findings.claim: Negative studies are under-published because of publication bias, not because they are usually poorly designed.
findings.evidence: "Negative studies ... may not be published. These results may due to the existence of questionable data or poorly designed studies."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Explain publication bias: well-designed negative trials matter and are often unpublished; trial registration reduces this.

findings.claim: Journal abstracts are usually limited to about 250-300 words, not 500.
findings.evidence: "usually contain ≤500 words."
findings.source: CONSORT for abstracts. Lancet 2008;371:281-3
findings.fix_hint: Say 'usually 250-300 words'.

findings.claim: The ADR type names are inconsistent and Type C is wrong: B is called 'Nonpharmacologic' then 'Bizarre'; C is called 'Continuous' then 'Chemical', with paracetamol hepatotoxicity as the example. In the standard scheme C is Chronic (dose- and time-related), e.g. HPA-axis suppression with corticosteroids.
findings.evidence: "Type B- (Nonpharmacologic) ... Type C- (Continuous)"; "Type C (Chemical) reactions ... Paracetamol: Hepatotoxicity."
findings.source: Edwards IR, Aronson JK. Adverse drug reactions: definitions, diagnosis, and management. Lancet 2000;356:1255-9
findings.fix_hint: One table A-F: Augmented, Bizarre, Chronic, Delayed, End of use, Failure, each with timing, dose relation and one example. Paracetamol overdose hepatotoxicity is Type A.

findings.claim: Pre-marketing trials miss rare ADRs; with about 3,000 patients a trial can detect roughly 1 in 1,000, so the '<1%' threshold is imprecise.
findings.evidence: "Cannot identify ADRs with incidence < 1%"
findings.source: Edwards IR, Aronson JK. Lancet 2000;356:1255-9
findings.fix_hint: "Rare ADRs (fewer than 1 in 1,000-10,000 patients) usually appear only after marketing (rule of three)."

findings.claim: The causality categories omit dechallenge (improvement on withdrawal), which WHO-UMC requires for 'certain' and 'probable'.
findings.evidence: "*Definite causality— ... re- administration of the medicine causes a similar reaction"
findings.source: WHO-UMC. The use of the WHO-UMC system for standardised case causality assessment. Uppsala Monitoring Centre; 2018
findings.fix_hint: Use the WHO-UMC table: certain, probable, possible, unlikely, conditional, unassessable; show time sequence, other causes, dechallenge and rechallenge as columns.

findings.claim: Errors of commission are not only due to lack of knowledge; slips and lapses also cause them.
findings.evidence: "2-Errors of Commission: a mistake that consists of doing something wrong due to Lack of knowledge ."
findings.source: NCC MERP. Taxonomy of Medication Errors; 2001
findings.fix_hint: "Commission: doing the wrong thing (wrong drug, dose, route or patient); omission: failing to do the right thing."

findings.claim: The FDA figure for brand-name review is unsourced and out of date.
findings.evidence: "FDA reviews 300 brand names in a year before they are marketed to avoid confusion of LASA drugs ."
findings.source: FDA Division of Medication Error Prevention and Analysis (DMEPA), current web page
findings.fix_hint: Say that the FDA screens every proposed proprietary name for look-alike/sound-alike risk before approval; drop the number.

findings.claim: The source is slide fragments with no learning objectives, summaries or connected explanation; text is broken into bullets and garbled tables (e.g. lines 837-948).
findings.evidence: "| -Strength | of the | association | . |"
findings.source: Instructional design standard (Anderson & Krathwohl 2001)
findings.fix_hint: Rewrite each section as a short guide: 'In This Section' objectives, tables and one flowchart, an 'At the Pharmacy' example, then 5 MCQs.

findings.claim: Causality is defined under 'The burden of ADRs', far from the causality section (lines 837-897).
findings.evidence: "The burden of ADRs / Causality: The probability that a particular medicine is responsible"
findings.source: Instructional design standard
findings.fix_hint: Move the definition to the causality chapter.

findings.claim: The biased-title example sits under a heading 'Blinding in Clinical Trials'.
findings.evidence: "Blinding in Clinical Trials / An example for a biased study title:"
findings.source: Instructional design standard
findings.fix_hint: Put the example under 'Title'.

findings.claim: The role of regulatory authorities in medication errors appears after the trauma case, cut off from the medication-error slides (lines 899-949).
findings.evidence: "*Role of regulatory authorities: • Important role in preventing medication errors ."
findings.source: Instructional design standard
findings.fix_hint: Move it into the medication-error part of the ADR chapters.

findings.claim: The list 'Reducing dispensing errors' mixes prescribing measures (electronic prescribing) with dispensing measures.
findings.evidence: "Reducing dispensing errors : 1- Electronic prescribing"
findings.source: ISMP. Key elements of medication use
findings.fix_hint: Group measures by stage: prescribing, dispensing, administration.

findings.claim: There are no MCQs, cases, exercises or answers in any section.
findings.evidence: No question appears in the source.
findings.source: Brief assessment (5 MCQs and one case per chapter)
findings.fix_hint: Write 5 single-best-answer MCQs (A-D) with one-line rationales and one practice case per chapter.

findings.claim: The source cites no references; statistics (ADR burden, PMC size, FDA names) have no source.
findings.evidence: "Studies have shown adverse drug reactions account for 1 in 16 hospital admissions"
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: 3-5 Vancouver references per chapter; cite Pirmohamed et al. BMJ 2004;329:15-9 for the ADR burden figures.

findings.claim: The PubMed Central size (4.8 million, dated 2018) is out of date; PMC now holds over 10 million articles.
findings.evidence: "Over 4.8 million articles are available." "10 June 2018"
findings.source: NCBI PMC home page (current)
findings.fix_hint: Say 'over 10 million full-text articles' or give no number.

findings.claim: There is no systematic approach to answering a drug information request (the core practical skill): get requester details, background, the real question, categorise, search, answer, follow up, document.
findings.evidence: "It is imperative that pharmacists know how to provide accurate and complete responses to DI requests."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022 (modified systematic approach, Host and Kirkwood)
findings.fix_hint: Add a 7-step flowchart with one worked request in Chapter 1.

findings.claim: Section 2 stops after secondary sources; primary literature (definition, types, pros and cons) is missing.
findings.evidence: "Secondary resources ... PubMed Central ... Google Scholar" (the deck ends here)
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Add primary literature: original research (trials, cohort, case reports); pros (most current, full detail) and cons (needs appraisal skill, may conflict).

findings.claim: The 'examples of tertiary drug sources' list gives question types but no named references.
findings.evidence: "*Example of tertiary drug sources : 1-General product information 2-Adverse effects ..."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Table: question type -> best reference (BNF / Martindale / AHFS; Meyler's; Stockley's; Briggs; Natural Medicines; Trissel's; Lexicomp Geriatric).

findings.claim: Drug information service is limited to requests from health professionals; patients and the public also ask.
findings.evidence: "problems that are received from health care professionals."
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
findings.fix_hint: Add patients and the public as requesters.

findings.claim: Section 8 ('Trauma') is a physiotherapy case of non-traumatic frozen shoulder; it has no drug-information question, source search or ADR content.
findings.evidence: "Diagnose Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) ... Mechanism of Injury: No history of trauma"
findings.source: Brief (Chapter 10: apply the whole course)
findings.fix_hint: Rebuild Chapter 10 as a pharmacy case: a DI request (e.g. NSAID choice and GI risk, or steroid injection), source search, evidence appraisal, a suspected ADR assessed with Naranjo, and a report.

findings.claim: Section 3 is missing: there is no content on study designs or the hierarchy of evidence between sources (Section 2) and randomisation (Section 4).
findings.evidence: Deck 2 ends at line 246; deck 4 starts at line 248.
findings.source: Brief (Chapter 3 added); Murad MH et al. New evidence pyramid. BMJ Evid Based Med 2016;21:125-7
findings.fix_hint: Add Chapter 3: case report/series, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, RCT, systematic review/meta-analysis; one table and the evidence pyramid.

findings.claim: Simple and blocked randomisation are listed but not explained; the unequal-allocation example is incomplete.
findings.evidence: "Simple method randomization. / Blocked randomization."
findings.source: CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869
findings.fix_hint: One table: method, how it works, when to use, one-line example.

findings.claim: Blinding is defined but single-, double- and triple-blind and allocation concealment are not explained.
findings.evidence: "Blinding keeps participants, clinical trial personnel ... unaware"
findings.source: CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869
findings.fix_hint: Add a who-is-blinded table and one line on allocation concealment.

findings.claim: p-value, confidence interval and the link between power and sample size are absent.
findings.evidence: "Gives detailed schedule of tests, procedures, medications, dosages, Sample size"
findings.source: Malone PM, Witt BA, Malone MJ, Peterson DM. Drug Information: A Guide for Pharmacists. 7th ed. McGraw Hill; 2022
